episode.episode: Philips Hue: The smart home’s light bulb moment
episode.showDescription: Version History is a show about the best gadgets ever. And the worst ones. And the ones that might have changed the world, if they ever actually shipped. Every week, your favorite people from The Verge and beyond hang out to tell and debate the story of a gadget, app, website, or any other tech product, and try to determine the item’s true legacy. Because not every product is a hit, but every product has a story. And the ones that really matter aren’t always the ones you think. From the Verge and the Vox Media Podcast Network.
episode.episodeDescription: The humble light bulb might be the ultimate success story in the smart home. Our connected, adaptable homes are supposed to be customizable, connected to everything, and incredibly easy to use, and nothing has made that work quite like Philips Hue lights. In this episode, The Verge's David Pierce and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy are joined by smart home journalist and expert Richard Gunther to tell the Hue's story. We trace the product's history from its origins in the smartphone revolution, try to figure out how Philips managed to turn a staggeringly expensive lightbulb into a must-have gadget, and look at whether there's even more invention left in the future of lighting. We’re also on video! Check us out on YouTube. Subscribe to The Verge for unlimited access to theverge.com, subscriber-exclusive newsletters, and our ad-free podcast feed. We love hearing from you! transcript_window.text: So and it was the right idea because obviously people loved it when it came.

I do think it was the right time because I don't think it would have I tried to do it later because I think the other reason that it was key was that iPhone because you suddenly had created a use case for something for a very hot, cool new device that everyone was interested in.
So you were really bringing all the pieces and parts together.
They just weren't quite there on the technology.
And so they kind of had to fudge it a little bit until the technology caught up.
So I guess you could maybe skid it a little bit down to wrong time.
But just a little bit, because if it could have if they could have done the bulb that came out two years later initially, then it would be smack back smack dab in right idea, right time, I think.
But they had to they had to compromise a little bit to get where they went.
Yeah.
Richard, you get to break the tie here.
What do you think?
I'm I'm all in.
I'm I'm right product, right time, right place.

I think that first mover advantage, particularly with regard to where the smart home was at the time when we started seeing all of these hubs pop up and all of these other ecosystems that people were playing with, they were there at the right time to be
the brand of choice for light bulbs.
And again, make fun of me if you must.
I used to attend an annual lighting conference called Light Fair.
Like a rent fair, but for lights.
But for lights.
And the number of companies that were dying out just trying to get the LED lighting, not even a smart bulb, but just trying to get the LED lighting correct.
I mean, there was a path of dead companies that had pretty good products but couldn't get there.
So I think they made the right move by going out with what they had and getting all these partnerships in place that they could then build on and iterate on.
And yeah, I'm all in.
That's good case.
I buy it.
All right.
